title: Chapter 25 – The Mending Fire
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

"A channel is a river," says Third Aunt Wenqing, "and a scarred channel is a river that has been dammed with its own mud."

She draws it for him on the back of a prescription sheet in the forge, with a stub of charcoal, while Old Hu snores and the three stones sit on the anvil like a clutch of pale eggs. A line, thick at one end, thin at the other, with a cluster of black crosshatching in the middle. "Your father's left side. Four main channels, and eight smaller, torn by the lynx when he was thirty-two. They healed, but badly. They healed shut. The Qi comes down from his shoulder and meets scar, and it either stops, or it goes around, and when it goes around it burns the tissue next to it. That is why his hand shakes."

"And the pill?"

"The old Green Pulse binds the walls so that the next surge does not tear them again. It is a bandage. It will not reopen a closed river." She taps the crosshatching. "What I need is something that will go into the scar, hold the edges apart, and let the Qi push through while it knits. Not mend a tear. Train one. Hold it open until the body forgets it was shut."

"Jade-vein fern."

"Your fern." She gives him a long look. "It conducts like meridian tissue. I would have said that was not possible if I had not held it in my hand. If the fern can stand in for the wall while the scar remembers how to be a river..." She shrugs. "Then he lifts a sword. Maybe."

"Maybe," says Lin Jian. He has already, privately, run the numbers. Thirty-eight to fifty-two percent. A coin tossed against the dark.

He picks up the charcoal and adds a second line, a thin one, beside the first. "And if it is not one pill, Third Aunt, but three? Spaced apart? The first holds it open. The second teaches it. The third..."

"Locks it in," says Wenqing slowly. "Yes."

"How long between?"

"A week. Perhaps three days more." She is looking at him now as she looked at him in the spring when he first told her about the fern. "You have thought about this."

"I read it somewhere," says Lin Jian, and does not look up.

* * *

The work moves to the stone hut.

There is a reason. A pill room with a bronze cauldron on the third floor of the main house is a pill room in plain sight of every cousin and servant, and Wenqing has already been asked twice what she is brewing at such an hour. Grandfather's answer, delivered with no particular expression, is to move the whole business into the old stone hut over the chamber stairs, in the middle of the twelve-pin ring, where nobody comes uninvited. A small furnace is bricked up in the corner. A bronze cauldron goes over it. A shelf, a bench, a lamp, a rack of jars.

And behind the cauldron, on a plain wooden table, where the smoke does not reach, the real work.

```
[ARK-7 :: Fabrication — Pill (variant of Green Pulse)]
Blueprint source: Wenqing formula (recorded), fern scan 61%
Stages: 1 Extract / 2 Bind / 3 Cool / 4 Seat
Reagents: jade-vein fern ×3, blood-stop grass, frostbell moss, cinnabar-iron (trace), mid-grade stone ×1
Estimated yield (blind run): 71%
Qi cost: 2.85 of 5.10
Failure mode: stage 3 (cooling), uneven; stage 4 (seating), Qi overshoot
```

Seventy-one percent. A pill that works seven times in ten is a pill that fails three, and he has three stones.

Do not run it blind.

It is the thing his old life taught him best. You do not weld a test piece on the real hull. You rehearse it, over and over, on a model that costs you nothing, until the rehearsal tells you where it breaks. He leans over the panel and asks the Interface the question it has not been asked before.

Run it as a dry pass. Don't burn the reagents.

```
DRY RUN available (Qi 0.40 per pass, no reagents consumed)
Simulate pass 1 / 2 / 3?
```

He runs it. The panel lays the four stages out in a ribbon, and the lamp seems to dim, and for a long moment the table in front of him is a table of ghosts: ghost fern, ghost grass, a ghost stone glowing at the center of a ghost cauldron. The ghosts move. They go through the four stages, and when the third stage comes, the ghost frostbell flares, and shrivels, and the whole ghost pill cracks down one side like a dropped plate.

```
Pass 1: FAIL (stage 3, cooling lag 1.4 s)
Pass 2: FAIL (stage 4, Qi overshoot 0.31)
Pass 3: SUCCESS 84%
Adjustment: add frostbell at stage 2.5, narrow stone channel to 0.62
```

Narrow the channel. A mid-grade stone does not release its Qi like a low-grade stone. It breaks the dam all at once, and the water goes everywhere. But there is a way to bleed it through a neck of the cauldron's own heat: a narrow throat, a measured trickle. He draws the neck on a scrap of paper. Hu, when he wakes and sees the scrap, grunts once and takes a file from the rack.

He runs the dry pass eleven times in the next two days. By the end, he knows that pill the way he once knew a weld.

* * *

The ingredients are another matter.

The fern is in the cleft. It has always been in the cleft: eleven plants, in a green crack of rock two hours south of the hill, where a waterfall drops into a pool so cold it burns the teeth. The cleft lies on the very edge of the foothills where the forest begins to thicken toward the Beast Mountains. Nobody goes there, because nobody has a reason, and because of the thing that lives under the ledge.

He told Kai about the fern in the spring. Kai, because he is Kai, offered to come. Kai is standing now on the ridge above the cleft, with his lance across his knees and his back to the water, having been told to keep watch for anyone coming from the south.

Lin Jian is not looking at Kai. He is looking at the ledge.

Rockshell badger, says the Scan, a moment after he thinks it. It is a pleasing, low-grade sort of beast. Stout as a barrel, covered in plates of gray horn that shed a spear like rain. First rank, medium tier. It has torn the moss off a good third of the cleft, which is the real problem, because the moss is the frostbell.

It could be avoided. He could ask Hu to come. Hu would take it down with a single swing of his rod and an offended expression. But Hu's rod is a loud tool, and the thing Lin Jian wants is not a dead badger. It is a rehearsal. In twenty-five days, three people will walk over the east ridge who are better than anything he has ever fought. He knows their names. He knows what they carry: the gaunt woman's wind blades, the man with the chain that dulls a fire spell, the narrow gray man with his poisoned darts. And he has never, in his life, been in a fight he did not prepare for with a month of lamplight.

So he prepares.

He goes down the cleft on the water side, quietly, with the Wind-Veil slip folded in his palm and the ash spear tucked across his back. The badger is dozing on its ledge. He steps out into the sun.

It wakes. It blinks small black eyes. It does not charge, because badgers do not. It rolls, a ball of plates, and comes at his ankles like a cart-wheel.

Falling Leaf. He steps. Three pale shapes of a boy peel away from his body, and the badger, which has the sort of mind that goes for the nearest warm thing, goes for the leftmost of them. It passes through a ghost with a snort of confusion and slams into the rock behind him. He has two breaths.

Now the wall. He slaps his palm to the ground, braiding the three threads Mao taught him. The earth rises, a low brown rampart, and he places it, not in front of him but behind the beast, where its roll will end. It uncurls, annoyed. It is in a ditch, and it is facing the wrong way.

Seam.

The Scan flickers across his vision as the badger turns.

```
[Scan — Rockshell Badger (first rank)]
Armor: horn plates, 3 mm
Weak point: underbelly seam, 11 cm behind forelimbs (unplated)
Behavior: rolls on threat; uncurls at 4–6 breaths
CE: +3 (total: 134 / 400)
```

The ash spear goes into the seam with a flat crunch. The badger lets out a long, offended wheeze and subsides.

He stands there for a moment with the spear in his hand and his heart hammering. It is not much of a victory. It is a first-rank beast the size of a calf. But the shape of it is right: draw it, wall it, strike the seam. The same rhythm, scaled up, will have to work on a woman who throws knives of wind. He does not know yet what he will substitute for the seam. He has a month.

"Jian?" calls Kai, from the ridge. "Are you all right?"

"I slipped!" he calls back.

"You slipped?"

"There was a badger."

A long silence. Then: "Is it dead?"

"It is very surprised," says Lin Jian.

By the time he has gathered the frostbell that the badger left, the moss is down to two clumps. He takes both. It will not be enough for three pills, and he knows it.

* * *

The first pill is ready on the eighth day.

It is the size of a pea, dark green, with a faint silver vein through the middle like a thread of mercury. It sits in a jade saucer on the stone hut's table, and the lamp makes a bead of light in its surface.

Father is lying on a pallet beside it, in his tunic, with his left arm bare to the shoulder. The scar-lattice runs down the skin like a spill of dark ink. Mother kneels at his head with her hands on his shoulders. Third Aunt stands at his feet. Grandfather sits cross-legged on the floor, with the flat stone of an anchor plate in his lap, and the glow of the twelve-pin ring comes up through the floor under him, a soft blue, as though the whole hut were floating in water.

"You are certain," Father says, to the ceiling.

"No," says Wenqing. "That is why we are doing it now, while the stones are fresh and your father's hand is on the ring."

"And if it fails?"

"Then it fails here, in the middle of the safest room on the hill, with the best healer in three valleys and a Patriarch at the end of your pulse." She lifts the pill with a pair of bamboo tongs. "Open."

He opens. It goes under his tongue.

For a moment, nothing. Then Father's breath catches, and his whole arm lifts off the pallet, the fingers curling, the knuckles standing out white, and Mother's hands on his shoulders go tight. A seam of faint green light crawls down his arm from the shoulder, following the black lines, and where it touches a scar the dark thread flickers and goes pale.

"It's holding," Wenqing says, very low. "It's holding. Wenyuan, don't fight it. Let it open."

Lin Jian stands against the wall with his hands in his sleeves, with his back to the stone, and does the only useful thing he can do, which is to count his father's breaths. Fifteen to the minute. Eighteen. Twenty-two. The Interface, somewhere at the back of his eyes, offers a thin gray line, and he reads it with half his attention and the other half on his father's face.

```
[Scan — Lin Wenyuan, left-side channels]
Scarred segments: 12 of 12 → 11 of 12 (1 partially open)
Qi throughput: 7% → 18%
Pain index: elevated, tolerable
Note: repeat dose in 3–4 days
```

Eleven of twelve. It is a small number, a modest advance, and the loveliest he has ever seen.

On the pallet, Father lets out a long, shaking breath, and Mother, who has not cried at a pyre or a funeral or the day they brought him home from the hunt with his arm in pieces, puts her forehead against his and does not say a word.

* * *

The second pill is ready on the eleventh day, and goes better still.

The third is a problem.

He has known it would be since the cleft. Two clumps of frostbell moss, enough for two pills if he is careful, and no third. He gathers every shred of the thing he can find within a day's walk; he scrapes the north side of every boulder on the hill, and Kai gives up and starts to laugh. He comes home with a pocketful of gray lichen that the Scan identifies, with some disappointment, as frostbell-adjacent, 14% cooling. It will not do.

"Cooling," says Lin Jian. "What else cools?"

"Ice," says Third Aunt, absently.

"What else?"

She considers. "A Fever-Cooling slip, I suppose. Your father's. But it only takes the edge off a fever. It would not touch a pill."

"Let me see one."

It is a plain Mortal-grade slip, gray paper and pale blue ink. He lays it on the bench beside the cauldron, and the dry run flickers over the two of them, the pill and the paper, and shows him what he suspected.

```
Pass 1: FAIL (cooling insufficient)
Pass 2: FAIL
Pass 3: SUCCESS 63% (Fever-Cooling slip burned at stage 3; yield reduced)
Risk: severe pain at seating; patient must be restrained
```

Sixty-three percent. A pill that works six times in ten, and when it works it hurts.

He tells Wenqing. She is silent for a long time, and then she says, "Your father will not agree if he knows."

"He doesn't have to know the number."

"Jian."

"I am not telling you to lie to him. I am telling you that he will take it either way." He looks at his hands. "He asked me to be the sort of person who knows where to cut. I would rather not cut with something blunt."

The third pill goes in on the fourteenth day, at night.

It is the worst hour of his life.

Father does not scream. That is the thing Lin Jian remembers afterward, with great clarity: that Lin Wenyuan, the best talisman drawer in three valleys, lies on a stone floor with his teeth locked, while the pill burns through the last of his scars from the inside, and does not make a sound. Mother holds his shoulders. Wenqing holds his wrist. Grandfather keeps the ring lit with a hand on the plate, and the blue glow goes up through the floor in pulses, and the light lurches in the hut like a boat in a storm.

It lasts an hour.

When it ends, Father is lying on his side with his eyes open, soaked to the skin, shaking from head to heel. He looks at the ceiling. He looks at Mother. He looks, at last, at the small figure by the wall.

"That," he says hoarsely, "was not in the formula."

"No," says Lin Jian. "I am sorry."

Wenyuan makes a sound that is almost a laugh. Then he lifts his left hand, slowly, carefully, from the stone, and holds it in front of his own face. It is steady. It is steady as a stone. He turns it over, once, and back.

"Qinghe," he says, "bring me my sword."

* * *

The result is forty-four percent.

Not the half that Wenqing had hoped for, and not the sixty-three that Lin Jian secretly believed in: a modest, lopsided, stubborn forty-four, of which Wenyuan recovers the use of two channels entirely, a third by half, and the rest by a scatter of thin new pathways that were not there before. He cannot rebuild what the lynx tore. But by the end of the third week, standing in the yard in the early morning with his tunic off and his old sword in his hand, he is for the first time in seven years a man who can lift it. He holds it at the guard for a hundred slow breaths. He walks through the opening forms of the Lin Blade, and when he reaches the end, he stands there for a long time with the point of the blade resting on the ground.

His Qi has come back to something like the third stage. Not his old fifth. Not a breakthrough. But a man.

Grandfather watches from the doorway. When Wenyuan finishes, the old man crosses the yard, not hurrying, and stops in front of his son. And then, without a word, in front of the whole morning household, Lin Zhenshan bows. Not the nod of a father. The full bow of a patriarch to a man.

Wenyuan, who has never in his life been bowed to, does not know where to put his sword.

"Hu's old formula," says Grandfather, to the courtyard at large. "From the book. I had no idea it would answer so well."

"Hu's old formula," agrees Third Aunt, with a straight face.

"Cooked," says Old Hu, from the forge door, "with a great deal of fetching and carrying. By a boy."

Several people laugh. Lin Wenyuan does not. He looks at Old Hu, and at Wenqing, and for the briefest moment at his youngest son, standing in the shade of the wall with his hands behind his back. And then he looks at his sword again, and says nothing, and Lin Jian understands that his father has decided, once and for all, to be a man who does not ask.

I have the best family in the world, he thinks. And not one of them is good at lying.

* * *

The Red Ridge report comes on the fifteenth day.

It arrives in the person of his mother, at dusk, in a peddler's wool cloak that smells of smoke and horse, with her hair under a rag and a basket of dried plums on her arm. She puts the basket on the kitchen table, takes off the cloak, and says to the room, "Get Feng. Get the Patriarch. Get your father."

She has been gone three days. Nobody knew where.

"Three," she says, when they are all around the table. "Hired. The river towns. A woman with a way of standing that tells you she has not lost a duel in ten years: wind, I think, from the sound of her. A man with a chain on his hip, a bright one, that I could feel from forty paces. And a thin man in a gray cloak who does not talk and does not blink." She lays three fingers on the wood. "All Qi Refining Eighth. All paid in full."

Nobody speaks.

"Zhao Qian drills the household guards in the south yard. Twenty-five of them. Mortal blades and some talismans. He is good at it." She turns her hand over. "Wenhai came in through the north gate on the second night after the council. He has not come out."

"Is he alive?" asks Father, quite quietly.

"I do not know." Su Qinghe looks at the table. "They have him in a room at the back of the east wing. There are two guards on the door. That is all I could learn."

Grandfather has not moved. He sits at the head of the table with his hands folded, as still as a man at prayer. At the end of it he nods, once.

"Twenty-five guards," he says. "Three Eighths. Zhao Qian at the Seventh. And Zhao Heng himself, who is a Foundation Establishment cultivator, and who may not come." He looks around the table at the faces of his family. "Thirty days ago I would have said we were dead. Today I think we are only outnumbered."

Feng laughs. It is a short, harsh sound, and he claps a hand over his mouth, and the table, one by one, begins to laugh with him, grimly, helplessly, like men at a funeral who have remembered a joke.

* * *

"Lin Hu says Grandfather is going to die."

Lin Yue says it on the stairs, in the evening, in the voice a five-year-old uses for a serious fact. She is sitting two steps up from him with her chin on her knees and her fern crown in her lap. She has been picking at the stalks.

He sits down beside her.

"Lin Hu says it's because of the pill," she continues. "He says that when old people take a pill like that, their hearts stop. His mother told him. He is sure."

She looks at him. Her eyes are very large and perfectly steady.

It would be the easiest thing in the world to lie. No, little one, nobody is going to die. She would believe it for a day. And then the day would come, and she would remember that he had said it.

"He might," says Lin Jian.

Lin Yue's face does not change.

"The pill is dangerous. He is very old. It could go wrong, and if it goes wrong, he might die." He keeps his voice even. "But he has asked me to help, and I am going to help him as much as I can. I cannot promise you that it will work. I can promise you that I am not going to stop."

She considers this for a long time. She turns the crown over in her hands.

"Okay," she says.

"Okay?"

"That's a better answer than Lin Hu's mother's." She sets the crown on his head, solemnly, askew. "You can have this. For luck."

He sits there for a minute, with the ferns scratching his ears, and cannot think of a single thing to say.

* * *

The last week goes in the forge.

There is a great deal to do, and not much time. Hu cuts the iron; Lin Jian draws the lines. Eighteen Azure Jade Nails come out of the brazier in a row, each the length of a finger, dull as lead, with a groove down the shank. They are not weapons. They are anchors. Each one, driven into the frame of a door, ties the pins around it into one net, so that a stranger crossing the threshold meets not one trap but all of them. He seats six in the main gate himself, working at night with a dark lantern, and reads each node through the Interface as it seats. Hu does the rest. Eight more pins go into the earth inside the gate. The anchor plate hums through all of them like a held breath.

On the last night he does one more thing.

Feng's practice sword hangs on its peg in the cadet yard, a plain steel blade, six years in use. It is good for its price, which is to say that it will hold an edge for a morning and a bend for a month. Lin Jian takes it down. He carries it to the forge when the fire is low and Hu is at his supper, and lays it on the anvil.

```
[Scan — Practice Sword, Lin Feng]
Material: steel, 0.7% carbon; micro-voids at 4 cm, 19 cm
Stress cracks (hairline): 3
Hardness: 52 HRC (target: 58)
SEPARATE available: inclusions (non-living, Level 2). Cost 3 CE (total after: 131 / 400)
```

Three hairline cracks, run through the steel like lines in a dry riverbed. He sets his fingertip to the blade, and the cracks lift out of it one by one with a faint metallic sigh, three bright slivers that fall onto the anvil and lie there like seeds. He quenches the edge in the cooling trough. The blade comes out the color of old silver.

When he hangs it on the peg again, it looks exactly as it did. But when Feng takes it down the next morning, and makes a pass in the air, his eyebrows go up.

"The book?" he says.

"The book," says Lin Jian.

Feng looks at him for a long time. Then he nods once, slowly, and does not say anything, and walks away with the sword.

* * *

The eve of midsummer is warm and still.

The whole valley seems to be holding its breath. Lin Jian sits on the wall above the north gate with his legs hanging over the edge and watches the light go out of the sky, copper, rose, violet. Below him, the nine pins lie in the dirt of the gate road like seeds waiting for rain. Behind him, in the yard, the family is eating a quiet supper; he can hear the clink of bowls.

He has one hundred and thirty-one points of CE and a Level 2 Interface. He has a spear, a knife, a bracelet, three talismans, and a clean pill in the chamber below the hall. He has two wind-slips, a pocketful of pins, and a wall that is better than it was. He has a month's practice on a badger.

It will not be enough. He knows that.

It will have to be.

"Lin Jian."

He turns.

Grandfather stands at the foot of the wall stair, in the dark. For a moment Lin Jian does not recognize him. The patched gray robe is gone. The old man wears the formal robe of the Patriarch, deep green, with the pine crest on the breast, and at his side, in a plain lacquered scabbard, hangs a sword. The blade is old and long and a little plain. Lin Jian has never seen him wear it.

"Come down, little builder," says Lin Zhenshan.

He climbs down. The old man is shorter than he seems in the chair; his head comes to the boy's eyes, almost, and the hand that settles on his shoulder is light as a leaf.

"Tomorrow is the longest day," he says. "Tomorrow I will take the pill. Whatever happens, tomorrow will be very loud." A pause. "Tonight there is something at the bottom of the forty steps that I want you to see."
